title: The Bracket Bet
primary_metric: after-tax value at retirement (USD) for each account type, as a function of the assumed future marginal tax rate

options.A: Pay Later — Traditional IRA: deduct the contribution this year, pay ordinary income tax on the full withdrawal (contributions plus all growth) at retirement
options.B: Pay Now — Roth IRA: pay tax on the contribution this year at today's known rate, owe nothing on the withdrawal at retirement

deliverables.text: An order-of-operations growth snapshot: the full expression for a single year's contribution grown 5, 15, and 30 years, evaluated step by step from raw multiplication, not a single plugged formula.
The forty-year growth ladder: a full compounding table for the investing horizon, in <=5-year increments, showing pre-tax balance growth is identical between Pay Later and Pay Now.
The two tax bills: after-tax value at retirement for both Pay Later and Pay Now under both Appendix D future-rate scenarios, with percent-of-a-number arithmetic shown for every tax bite.
The crossover chart: an original visual display graphing after-tax retirement value against assumed future tax rate for both options, marking both D3 scenarios and any crossover.
A recommendation memo naming the single number the recommendation depends on most, and what value would flip it.

balance.argument_a: CONFIRMED by case-research. Pay Later (Traditional) wins under Scenario 2 (future rate 10%, lower than today's 12%): after-tax value $1,599,480 vs. Roth's $1,563,936 -- a 2.3% margin. The deduction today is worth today's (higher) 12% rate, while the eventual tax bite is assessed at the lower 10% future rate on the same dollars.
balance.argument_b: CONFIRMED by case-research. Pay Now (Roth) wins under Scenario 1 (future rate 22%, higher than today's 12%): after-tax value $1,563,936 vs. Traditional's $1,386,216 -- a 12.8% margin. Paying tax once, now, at a known 12% rate beats paying tax later on a much larger balance at 22%.
balance.margin_basis: Computed after-tax retirement value for both options under Appendix D's Scenario 1 and Scenario 2 (D3), using C=$3,000/yr, r=10%, n=43 years, FV (annuity) ~= $1,777,200. Traditional after-tax = FV x (1 - r_future); Roth after-tax = FV x (1 - r_today). Full arithmetic in RESEARCH_LOG.md.
balance.candidate_rate_scenario_for_research: RESOLVED. The originally-floated candidate anchored Devon's current bracket at 10-12% and set Scenario 1 two brackets higher near 22%, holding Scenario 2 flat or one bracket lower. Verifying against the real 2026 IRS bracket table (Devon's assumed ~$40,000 entry-level salary, BLS-anchored, minus the $16,100 standard deduction = ~$23,900 taxable income) placed Devon's ACTUAL current bracket at 12%, not 10% -- which matters, because anchoring at 10% (the bottom of the schedule) would have left no real published bracket below it for the required 'lower' counter-scenario, an internal contradiction in the original candidate. With current bracket confirmed at 12%, the real bracket one step up (22%) and one step down (10%) were used directly -- no invented percentages, and the two scenarios still straddle today's rate in both directions as SPEC requires. Resulting margins: 12.8% (Scenario 1, Roth wins) and 2.3% (Scenario 2, Traditional wins), both comfortably inside the ~20% cap -- no landslide, no retune of contribution amount or return rate was needed. See RESEARCH_LOG.md for the full verification arithmetic.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Devon's current marginal federal tax bracket
modeling_assumptions.basis: Not itself an assumption -- computed from the real, current 2026 IRS bracket table (S8) against Devon's assumed entry-level income (~$40,000, S1) less the $16,100 standard deduction. Carried in the Modeling Assumptions block as context for MA2/MA3.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Fixed; not a free variable in the case.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Assumed future marginal tax bracket at retirement, Scenario 1 (rates rise)
modeling_assumptions.basis: A real, currently-published federal bracket (S8), one step above Devon's current 12%. Chosen as a realistic mid-to-late-career trajectory over a ~43-year working life.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Roth wins by ~12.8% under this scenario. If the true future rate were 24% or higher, Roth's margin widens; at exactly 12% the two options tie.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Assumed future marginal tax bracket at retirement, Scenario 2 (rates fall or stay low)
modeling_assumptions.basis: The real bottom bracket of the federal schedule (S8), one step below Devon's current 12%. Chosen as the required realistic counter-scenario (a modest, largely Social-Security-supported retirement income) so the case cannot be resolved by assuming taxes only ever rise.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Traditional wins by ~2.3% under this scenario -- a very tight margin. At exactly 12% the two options tie.

sensitivity_note: The entire dilemma is a sensitivity study by design: the primary metric is defined as a function of the assumed future tax rate specifically because the answer flips depending on it. FACILITATOR.md records which direction favors which option and the candidate research target; case.md never states which scenario wins.
reinforcement_note: All 6 claimed skills already show n>0 in readmodel/standards_spine.json at write time (Exponent/Base/Percent terms and their three how-to skills range from n=2 to n=63), so new_coverage[] is correctly empty per SPEC §4's literal n==0 rule. This case was approved from the concept sheet specifically to reinforce the thin advanced-operations-how-to-evaluate-an-expression-with-multiple-operations-with-exponents-order skill (n=2, tied for the thinnest how-to in the Advanced Operations/Exponents group) by forcing it twice (D1 and D2), not to close a zero-coverage gap -- consistent with the concept sheet's own framing ('genuinely closes the thin ... skill') and with the precedent set in cases/the-bracket-cliff/LEARNING_GOALS.md and cases/prove-it-scales/case.json for disclosed reinforcement-only cases. Flag for case-qa to confirm this disclosed deviation rather than treat it as an undisclosed zero-new-coverage defect.
balance_test_risk_note: RESOLVED at case-research (2026-09-03). The Tier-1 T1-09 balance risk flagged at write time did not materialize as a landslide: verifying the candidate bracket pair against the real, current 2026 IRS bracket table found Devon's actual current bracket is 12% (not 10% as originally floated), which corrected the candidate scenario -- 22% (Scenario 1, one bracket up) and 10% (Scenario 2, one bracket down) are both real published brackets that still straddle 12% in both directions. Computed margins: 12.8% (Roth wins, Scenario 1) and 2.3% (Traditional wins, Scenario 2), both comfortably inside SPEC §2's ~20% cap -- no MCS-46 waiver needed, and no retune of Appendix A's contribution amount or Appendix B's return rate was required. Full verification arithmetic in RESEARCH_LOG.md.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA2 (assumed future marginal tax bracket, Scenario 1) is a forecast of a real human tax bracket decades from now -- irreducible unknown, not knowable in advance by any amount of research (case.json.sensitivity_note; FACILITATOR.md Sensitivity note). P5 finds -50% flex (22% -> 11%) flips the verdict to Traditional and +50% flex (22% -> 33%) pushes Roth's margin past the 20% cap; both are the case's own designed point, not an authoring defect -- case.md already forces every reader to compute both Appendix D scenarios (D3) and D5 explicitly asks for the exact number that would flip the recommendation. This is the case's entire reason to exist, already disclosed in case.md's structure, case.json.balance, and FACILITATOR.md's Balance argument and Sensitivity note -- not a hidden fragility.
